interactive.title: Stretch and turn
interactive.whatAmILookingAt: A short lesson in thirteen small screens on the complex plane from the last lesson, real across and j up. An arrow z runs from 0 to a dot you can drag, and beside it a dashed arrow, jz, is the same arrow turned a quarter turn anticlockwise. Two sliders set c and d, the parts of a second number c + jd. The product z × (c + jd) is built in front of you: c lots of z laid from 0, then d lots of jz laid on its tip, and the arrow from 0 to where they end is the answer, because multiplying out the bracket gives c times z plus d times jz. Under the arrows sits the four-tile grid from Quadratics, one tile for each part times each part. The j × j tile slides across to the real pile with its sign changed, because j × j = −1. Some screens show an idea and the rest ask you to try it: a puzzle offers three answers, a wrong pick gets a one-line hint naming its slip, and Why? replays the arrows and tiles for it.
interactive.ignores: The dots snap to whole steps so the parts can be counted, but a complex number's parts can be any numbers. The tiles keep count of the four products the way Quadratics did; here they are bookkeeping, not areas, since a j part is not a length on the ground. The picture shows that every arrow gets the same stretch and the same turn; giving that stretch and turn as a length and an angle is a later lesson.

explain.text:
Multiplying two complex numbers works like multiplying out two brackets, with one extra step: wherever j × j appears, put −1. On the plane, the answer is the first arrow stretched and turned. Later lessons use it to work out the currents and voltages of AC circuits.

Times a positive number stretches or shrinks an arrow without turning it: 2 × (2 + j1) = 4 + j2, both parts doubled, so it points the same way and is twice as long. Times −1 turns it through 180 degrees.[^1] Times j turns it a quarter turn anticlockwise.[^2] Multiply out to see why: j × (2 + j1) = j2 + j × j × 1 = −1 + j2. The real part 2 has become j2, so it now points up, and the j part j1 has become −1, so it now points left. In the last lesson an arrow was its across part and its up part laid tip to tail, so turning both pieces a quarter turn turns the corner they make, and the arrow with it. The same happens to any arrow: j × (a + jb) = −b + ja, the same two sizes swapped, so by Pythagoras the turned arrow is just as long.

Now two brackets, as the four tiles in Quadratics: (3 + j2)(1 + j2). The tiles are 3 × 1 = 3, 3 × j2 = j6, j2 × 1 = j2 and j2 × j2 = j × j × 4 = −4. That last tile started as two j parts multiplied, but j × j = −1 makes it a real number, so it moves to the real pile with its sign changed. The rules are the ones for ordinary brackets, plus j² = −1.[^3] Real: 3 − 4 = −1. j: 6 + 2 = 8. The answer is −1 + j8. Take j × j as +1 and you get 7 + j8, a different arrow. This is the difference from adding: adding keeps real with real and j with j, while multiplying moves a piece across.

Why is the answer a stretch and turn? Split the second bracket: z × (c + jd) is c lots of z plus d lots of jz, laid tip to tail. Since jz is z turned a quarter turn, those two pieces make a right-angled corner, c lots along z and d lots across it. The number c + jd is the same corner, c across and d up, drawn from 1 instead of from z. So the answer is c + jd's corner laid along z at z's size: whatever turn and stretch takes 1 to c + jd takes z to the answer. For (2 + j1)(1 + j1), z + jz = (2 + j1) + (−1 + j2) = 1 + j3, while 1 goes to 1 + j1. By Pythagoras 1 + j1 is √2, about 1.41, long, and 2 + j1 grows from √5, about 2.24, to √10, about 3.16, which is 2.24 × 1.41: the same stretch. A later lesson turns this into a rule with lengths and angles.[^4] **Multiply out the brackets and put −1 for j × j;[^3] the answer is the first arrow stretched and turned.**

analogy.text: Think of putting a wiring drawing on the office copier at 200%, with the sheet turned a quarter turn on the glass. Every cable run on it comes out twice as long and turned the same way, whatever direction it ran. Multiplying every arrow by j2 does the same: each one is doubled and turned a quarter turn anticlockwise.
analogy.breaks: The copier has two separate settings, size and turn, while one complex number sets both at once: 1 + j1 stretches by about 1.41 and turns an eighth of a turn. And on a copy only the shapes and their directions matter, wherever they sit on the sheet, while multiplying swings every point round 0, so a point far from 0 moves a long way.

practice.text:
- Write both numbers as a + jb, with a sign in front of each part.
- Multiply every part of the first by every part of the second: four tiles.
- Put −1 for each j × j, so that tile moves to the real pile with its sign changed.
- Add the real tiles, then the j tiles. Write the real part first.
- Check on a sketch: the answer should be the first arrow turned and stretched the way 1 is turned and stretched into the second number.

**Rule of thumb:** Times j is a quarter turn anticlockwise, times −j a quarter turn clockwise, times −1 a half turn. Times a positive number only stretches or shrinks.

**Worked example:** (3 − j2)(2 + j5). Tiles: 3 × 2 = 6, 3 × j5 = j15, −j2 × 2 = −j4, and −j2 × j5 = −j × j × 10 = +10. Real: 6 + 10 = 16. j: 15 − 4 = 11. The answer is 16 + j11. Check with arrows: 2 lots of (3 − j2) is 6 − j4; j × (3 − j2) = j3 + 2 = 2 + j3, and 5 lots of that is 10 + j15; laid tip to tail they end at 16 + j11.

**Common mistakes**
- Taking j × j as +1. (2 + j3)(1 − j2) is 8 − j1, not −4 − j1.
- Multiplying real by real and j by j only, as if adding. That gives 2 − j6 for the same product and skips two tiles.
- Losing a sign on −j × j. It is −(j × j) = +1.
- Squaring each part and dropping the middle tiles, instead of drawing all four tiles as in Quadratics. (1 − j1)² is −j2, not 0.

checks.label: Multiplying a number by j is a rotation by +90 degrees: on Times j the arrow 2 + j1 and its two parts swing a quarter turn anticlockwise about 0 at full length, ending on −1 + j2 with the real part 2 now pointing up, the turn drawn as 90°

If a number is multiplied by −1, its vector is turned through 180 degrees: on Stretching the arrow 2 + j1 swings half round about 0 at full length to −2 − j1, both parts changed in sign, the turn drawn as 180°

Multiplication follows the rules of normal algebra plus j² = −1: on every grid the tiles, part times part, with the j × j tile moved to the real pile with its sign changed, add up to the product, as (3 + j2)(1 + j2) = −1 + j8 and (2 + j3)(1 − j2) = 8 − j1

To multiply two numbers, multiply their lengths (moduli) and add their turns (arguments): on Same stretch, same turn, the answer is as long as z and c + jd multiplied, and turned from z exactly as far as c + jd is turned from 1, both turns marked alike
Each puzzle takes only its right answer: every answer is named for where its arrows or tiles land, and each wrong one lands somewhere else

Drag z and move c and d: for every c and d from −2 to 2 and every z tried, c lots of z then d lots of jz, laid tip to tail, end on z × (c + jd), jz is z turned a quarter turn, the tiles add up to the same answer, and every arrow stays on the plane
Before an answer, a puzzle shows only the question: its arrow or empty tiles, with no answer, no copies, no turn and no tile moved
Every demonstration finishes within 4.6 s of its screen opening, none starting before the 0.35 s screen fade ends; every answer's motion, right or wrong, within 3 s

From outside the rule: four quarter turns bring an arrow home (j × j × j × j = 1); a quarter turn swaps the two sizes, so by Pythagoras the turned arrow is just as long, for every whole-step arrow tried; and the worked example (3 − j2)(2 + j5) = 16 + j11 comes out the same by tiles and by arrows

applied.problem: "Later lessons multiply the currents and voltages of AC circuits this way" says current is multiplied by voltage; the later lessons multiply a current by an impedance (V = IZ) to find a voltage, and never multiply V by I.
"Squaring each part and dropping the middle tiles, as in Quadratics" reads as if Quadratics taught dropping the middle tiles; Quadratics drew all four tiles, and (a + b)² is not a² + b².

notes.problem: Step 4 slip "parts swapped, minus on the wrong one" gives real part −3, i.e. −3 + j1, but that answer keeps 3 and 1 in place (a mirror in the j axis); swapped with the minus on the wrong part is 1 − j3. The build should word that hint to match the wrong answer shown.
